catalog_quote: This research work describes the aspects of Kuturmi phonology. It examines the sound system and patterns of Kuturmi language and the phonological process that are found in the language. ... Chapter two presents the sounds, types of syllable and syllable processes of Kuturmi language. It also deals with the charts of both consonant and vowel sounds. Chapter three examines the phonological processes like assimilation, deletion, insertion, nasalization and vowel harmony that are attested in the language. Chapter four presents the tone and tonological processes of the language. It also gives detailed information on the types of tone attested in Kuturmi language. ... [sec. 1.8.1] The informant method and frame technique was used in this research while the native speaker served as a source of information as well as the means of evaluation of all sounds and tones present in the language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated anywhere accessible. The only phonological description of Kuturmi (an Ilorin 2011 thesis, seen in Chapter-1 preview) treats the language as tonal — a whole chapter on 'tone and tonological processes' and 'types of tone attested' — and does not mention stress in the parts that can be read. Blench's 2006 wordlist has an empty 'Tones' heading and says nothing about stress either.
new_statements.exceptions: None; nothing on stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Chapter outline only; the tone chapter itself (Ch. 4) is paywalled and unread, so whether it says anything about stress, or about the domain of tone (word vs phrase), is unknown. Thesis data are from Awon (the 'standard' dialect) informants; Blench's wordlist is from Anturu village.
new_statements.identity_note: Kuturmi = Ada (Glottolog alt. name) = Ibiro-Ikryo (Blench Atlas per Wikipedia; dialects Ikryo/West and Ibiro/East). The Ilorin phonology thesis names Awon as the standard dialect and lists Anturu, Akama, Ariko, Awon, Asane, Akwando; the verb-phrase thesis names dialects Inuwa (Awon) and Umsuwe (Arikwo); Blench's 2006 wordlist is from Anturu village. All fall under kutu1262; no separate glottocodes for the dialects.

sources.note: The only phonological description of Kuturmi. Ch. 2 covers syllable structure, Ch. 4 tone and tonological processes; it is the one place a statement on stress (or an explicit 'tonal, no stress') would exist. Only the Chapter-1 preview is open; Chapters 2-5 are sold at N3,000 / $8 by a Nigerian project-sale site (no DOI); print copy at the University of Ilorin only — no HathiTrust/IA/Harvard record.
